items.title: Extended reality visual language for professional contexts: a study on visual dissonance
items.abstract: Abstract Extended Reality (XR) is increasingly deployed in professional workflows, where adoption research has focused on hardware ergonomics and cybersickness. As these barriers are addressed, an open question concerns how such interfaces should be visually designed. Professional XR often inherits the visual register of consumer systems, with saturated palettes, gamified treatments, and stylized characters that may conflict with workplace norms. We define this mismatch as visual dissonance, and professionally aligned designs as native visual language. Established acceptance models capture the social conditioning of adoption through generic normative beliefs, but carry no construct for the visual channel that signals workplace conventions in an immersive medium. This study examines whether visual dissonance undermines perceived credibility across three XR interface components: workspace layouts, avatar representations, and data dashboards. A within-subject survey (N = 96) compared paired aligned and dissonant stimuli with functional content held constant. Sensitivity proves component-specific rather than a single dispositional trait. When asked which variant they would trust professionally, participants selected the aligned one for both avatars and dashboards, at rates that did not differ between these two components, while for workspace layouts the choice was balanced. When each variant was rated separately, only avatars showed a reliable difference: the dashboard effect appears only when a choice is required. Graded self-report alone may underestimate visual effects; XR familiarity amplifies rather than reduces sensitivity. These findings position the visual register of professional XR as a measurable adoption factor to be evaluated component by component and through both measurement channels.

items.title: Extra-Role Behavior in Organizations: A Thematic Synthesis of the Most Cited Studies
items.abstract: Introduction: Although extra-role behavior is widely recognized as a decisive factor in organizational efficiency, current literature remains highly fragmented across disciplines. This fragmentation hinders a cohesive understanding of its antecedents and consequences. To address this gap, this study systematically examines the core themes, relational structures, and accompanying variables present in the foundational literature on extra-role behavior. Method: Following PRISMA guidelines, a qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis were conducted on the fifty-two most highly cited publications indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) Core Collection. Data collection was carried out between April-May 2026. Results or Findings: Findings reveal that the antecedents and consequences of extra-role behavior cluster into four primary dimensions as leadership dynamics, individual psychological drivers, organizational climate and job design, and negative dynamics. While extra-role behavior flourishes under positive leadership paradigms, job autonomy, and intrinsic psychological states, the findings also reveals a critical dark side. Specifically, excessive formalization and perceived compulsory citizenship suppress voluntary behavioral tendencies and increase employee burnout. Discussion or Conclusion: This research helps to better understand the concept of the extra role by bringing together fragmented findings in the literature. In doing so, it provides decision-makers with actionable strategic insights to encourage voluntary employee behavior.

items.title: From AI Adoption to AI-Augmented Work: How AI-Enabled HRM Shapes Hospitality Employee Well-Being through Job Redesign and Work Autonomy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in hospitality organisations, yet research has often concentrated on adoption, acceptance and service-robot reactions rather than on how AI changes the design and experience of work. This study develops an employee-centred model explaining how AI-enabled human resource management (AI-HRM) can influence hospitality employee well-being through AI-enabled job redesign and work autonomy, while examining AI self-efficacy as an individual boundary condition. Drawing on Conservation of Resources theory and the Job Demands?Resources framework, the model proposes a resource-gain pathway in which AI-enabled HRM facilitates redesign of tasks and roles, redesigned work enhances autonomy, and autonomy improves employee well-being. The proposed empirical design uses a three-wave survey of employees in AI-exposed hospitality organisations. For analytical prototyping, an empirical dataset of 450 cases was examined using reliability analysis, descriptive statistics, discriminant-validity diagnostics, regression-based structural paths, 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation and interaction analysis. The prototype results show strong internal consistency and a positive serial indirect pathway from AI-HRM to well-being through job redesign and autonomy. However, the moderation interaction is small and statistically non-significant in the observed data. The study's substantive contribution is to reposition AI-HRM from a technology-adoption question toward a human-centred work-design question.

items.title: How can AI accelerate the green transition?
items.abstract: In his essay The Gift, published in 1925, the sociologist Marcel Mauss emphasised the 'total' scope of the phenomenon of gift-and counter-gift-giving, noting that it 'expresses, simultaneously and all at once, all manner of institutions: religious, legal and moral (...)\,; economic (...)\,; not to mention the aesthetic phenomena to which these facts give rise (...).'' The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), which is suddenly and profoundly disrupting individual and collective lives, bears a resemblance to the ''total social fact'' described a hundred years ago. AI refers to technologies designed to simulate human intelligence, namely an ''automated system that (...) deduces, from received inputs, how to generate output results such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that may influence physical or virtual environments.'' 4 (OECD). Having become central to human relations, AI relies on physical and globalised infrastructure and therefore, also has an impact on the environment. This paper analyses some of these effects and how they are perceived by society. This text offers an exploration of the links between AI and the ecological transition, seeking to identify new opportunities and constraints. To this end, it will identify the barriers to the ecological transition (1) and the environmental impacts attributable to AI (2). It will then go on to describe how to live in a constrained world (3) while AI accelerates scientific discovery (4) and profoundly transforms society (5).

items.title: Human Factors in Aircraft Maintenance: Linking Occupational Motivation, Work Alienation, and Flow Experience
items.abstract: Today's aviation maintenance environments place significant cognitive and psychological demands on aircraft maintenance technicians due to increasing fleet size, intense operational pace, and extremely low tolerance for error. In this context, understanding the psychological and motivational processes that shape the human performance of maintenance personnel is critical for the sustainability of flight safety. This study aims to examine the relationships between work alienation, occupational motivation, and work-related flow in aircraft maintenance technicians within a holistic model framework. The research was conducted using data from 207 aircraft maintenance technicians. Descriptive and correlational analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 31). The proposed research model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) via the SEM module of Jamovi (version 2.7.6) software and the lavaan package running in the R environment. The mediating role of occupational motivation was evaluated using the bootstrap resampling method. The findings show that work alienation significantly and negatively affects occupational motivation and work-related flow experience; while occupational motivation positively predicts work-related flow. Mediation analyses revealed that occupational motivation plays a partial mediating role in the relationship between work alienation and work-related flow. The results indicate that human performance in maintenance settings should be considered not only from the perspective of technical competence and error management, but also by taking into account motivation and psychological attachment processes.

items.title: Human Factors in Data Preparation
items.abstract: Data preparation is a cornerstone of the data science lifecycle, yet it remains one of the most time-consuming and human-dependent stages. Human factors are critical here, shaping how users interact with tools, perceive data quality, and make trade-offs under uncertainty. At the crossroads of Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), Visualization, and human-in/over-the-loop paradigms, recent research highlights new opportunities to make data preparation more usable, transparent, and trustworthy. Interactive interfaces and visual analytics systems allow users to iteratively refine transformations, explore provenance, and detect anomalies, while cognitive aspects such as workload, bias, and trust determine the reliability of human interventions. Automation increasingly complements these workflows: human-in-the-loop methods leverage user feedback to guide cleaning, labeling, or schema alignment, and over-the-loop frameworks provide oversight mechanisms to prevent over-reliance on automation. At the same time, modern generative AI introduces powerful new capabilities, such as automatically suggesting transformations, synthesizing metadata or documentation, and even generating realistic synthetic datasets. These advances promise efficiency and creativity but raise concerns about reliability, explainability, and provenance, reinforcing the need for careful human oversight. This chapter reviews these possibilities and the research challenges in developing a new class of hybrid, adaptive data-preparation solutions that blend human expertise with automated intelligence. Key challenges include balancing scalability with user effort, ensuring transparency in automated suggestions, preventing loss of situational awareness, and developing evaluation metrics that reflect both human experience and technical accuracy. Addressing these challenges will enable more robust, human-aware data preparation practices across domains.

items.title: Impact of Multimedia Display Technologies on Visual Fatigue and Learning Effectiveness
items.abstract: The rapid transition from traditional to digital education has significantly transformed teaching and learning processes. Modern classrooms are now equipped with multimedia technologies such as interactive boards, projectors, and internet-enabled tools, making education more flexible and accessible. However, the excessive use of digital technology has introduced new challenges, particularly digital fatigue among students. Digital fatigue is characterized by mental exhaustion resulting from prolonged screen exposure, repetitive digital content consumption, and limited face-to-face interaction. The increasing reliance on digital platforms has been associated with reduced motivation, lower efficiency, and heightened stress among students. Prolonged screen use can also lead to physiological issues such as headaches, eye irritation, difficulty concentrating, and sleep disturbances, commonly referred to as digital eye strain. In addition to physical effects, digital learning environments contribute to psychological challenges, including anxiety, emotional exhaustion, and burnout, which negatively affect students’ academic performance and overall well-being. Sleep disruption further exacerbates these problems, as excessive screen time interferes with rest and recovery. Moreover, the lack of clear boundaries between academic and personal time in digital settings can result in continuous mental strain. The physical classroom environment also plays a crucial role, as factors such as improper lighting, glare, and poor viewing distances can intensify visual discomfort and fatigue. While multimedia technologies enhance interactivity and accessibility in education, their unregulated use may adversely affect students’ cognitive, visual, and emotional health. Despite the implementation of hybrid learning models, there remains a need for more structured and effective strategies to address digital fatigue. This study highlights the importance of promoting digital well-being through balanced technology use, ergonomic practices, and improved classroom design.

items.title: Inteligencia Artificial con Alma: Modelo Humanista para una Transformación Digital Ética, Confiable y Orientada al Bienestar
items.abstract: Objective: To formulate and substantiate the “Artificial Intelligence with Soul” model as a humanistic framework for governing, designing, adopting, and evaluating artificial intelligence systems in organizations and universities. Methodology: A theoretical-propositional study was conducted through an integrative review of literature on trustworthy artificial intelligence, algorithmic ethics, human-centered design, sociotechnical systems, digital well-being, data justice, explainability, human oversight, and risk management. International regulatory and technical frameworks were compared, including UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act. Results: A multilevel model is proposed comprising six principles—legitimate purpose, dignity and rights, human agency, justice and inclusion, sociotechnical trustworthiness, and sustainable well-being—four governance layers—strategic, organizational, technical, and relational—and a 4A activation cycle: Learning, Attitude, Soul, and Action. The article contributes an assessment matrix, twelve testable propositions, an indicator dashboard, a preliminary 36-item scale, and an implementation roadmap. Conclusions: Responsible AI cannot be reduced to regulatory compliance or technical accuracy. It requires alignment among purpose, data, architecture, decisions, power relations, and human consequences. The model translates ethical principles into verifiable practices and offers a research agenda for validating its usefulness across sectors and cultural contexts.

items.title: Managers Who Build and Managers Who Break: Abusive Supervision, Psychological Safety, and Team Learning-A Critical Review of the Evidence and Its Limits
items.abstract: In normal language, it's just one word that makes the difference between a manager and a damager, but the difference in behaviour between the two can be measured in the learning of the team, the health of the staff and the cost to the organisation. This article examines peer-reviewed journal evidence pertaining to supervisory behavior, including studies on abusive supervision, psychological safety, just culture in safety critical industries, and occupational health research that relates supervisors' ratings to reported illness. These can be found in occupational medicine cohort studies, regulatory text on error reporting and the use of data in the workplace, and in organisational behaviour journals and international standards on psychosocial risk. Three findings recur. First, teams which have leaders who ask how when things go wrong report more problems and make earlier corrections than teams with leaders who ask who. Second, hostile supervision is positively related to turnover intentions, decreased task performance and poorer health, with most designs being based on employee perception and there is limited ability to determine cause and effect. Third, the published figures of cost of damaging supervision are less convincing than the fact that they are frequently cited is sometimes thought to indicate. This article outlines the current measurement options, the legal parameters for their use, and practical options for employers, regulators, and employees. The evidence of causation and cross-country data are still relatively scarce.

items.title: Más Allá de la Salud: Modelo Integral de Felicidad, Bienestar y Florecimiento Humano
items.abstract: Objective: To substantiate a multidimensional model that expands health toward happiness, well-being, and flourishing by integrating personal, relational, material, and digital factors. Methodology: A theoretical-propositional study supported by an integrative review of the biopsychosocial model, subjective and eudaimonic well-being, self-determination, positive psychology, meaning, social determinants, capabilities, occupational health, and digital well-being. Results: The Integral Model of Human Well-Being with Soul (MIBHA) is formulated around eight dimensions—body, thought, emotions, transcendence, social life, professional life, finances, and technology—and five cross-cutting mechanisms: resources, agency, regulation, connection, and meaning. A theory of change, ten propositions, a preliminary 40-item scale, indicators, implementation phases, and ethical safeguards are developed. Conclusions: Well-being cannot be reduced to a score, an individual habit, or the absence of disease. It requires real capabilities, fair environments, and responsible governance. MIBHA offers a testable basis for research and intervention without replacing clinical diagnosis or treatment. Its original contribution lies in separating life domains from cross-cutting mechanisms, treating technology as a constitutive dimension, and introducing a non-compensation principle for severe deprivation.

items.title: MOTIVATIONAL STRATEGIES OF SCIENCE TEACHERS AND STUDENT GRADE PERFORMANCE BASIS FOR INTERVENTION PROGRAM
items.abstract: The motivational strategies used by Science teachers and their relationship with students’ engagement and academic performance were assessed in this study as a basis for an intervention program. The study was conducted from June to November 2025. It examined teachers' use of intrinsic and extrinsic motivational strategies, students' behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, their academic performance in Science, and their relationships. Quantitative descriptive-correlational research was conducted to 147 Grade 7 learners. Validated survey questionnaires and academic grade performance in Science were utilized to collect data. Descriptive statistics, such as the weighted mean and standard deviation, were used to characterize the variables, while Spearman’s rho was used to assess relationships among motivational strategies, student engagement, and academic grade performance. The results indicated that science teachers actively used extrinsic and intrinsic motivational strategies. Most students demonstrated behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, and their first-quarter performance in Science showed strong academic competence. Furthermore, the intrinsic and extrinsic motivational strategies had a weak positive, statistically significant link with grade performance. However, no significant association was identified between the motivational strategies and students' behavioral, emotional, or cognitive engagement. The study indicates that motivational strategies have some impact on students’ academic performance, but the effect is very limited. The study led to the development of the Science Motivation and Engagement Enhancement Program (SMEEP) as an intervention to improve students’ motivation, engagement, and academic achievement in Science. items.title: MOTIVATIONAL STRATEGIES OF SCIENCE TEACHERS AND STUDENT GRADE PERFORMANCE BASIS FOR INTERVENTION PROGRAM
items.abstract: The motivational strategies used by Science teachers and their relationship with students’ engagement and academic performance were assessed in this study as a basis for an intervention program. The study was conducted from June to November 2025. It examined teachers' use of intrinsic and extrinsic motivational strategies, students' behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, their academic performance in Science, and their relationships. Quantitative descriptive-correlational research was conducted to 147 Grade 7 learners. Validated survey questionnaires and academic grade performance in Science were utilized to collect data. Descriptive statistics, such as the weighted mean and standard deviation, were used to characterize the variables, while Spearman’s rho was used to assess relationships among motivational strategies, student engagement, and academic grade performance. The results indicated that science teachers actively used extrinsic and intrinsic motivational strategies. Most students demonstrated behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, and their first-quarter performance in Science showed strong academic competence. Furthermore, the intrinsic and extrinsic motivational strategies had a weak positive, statistically significant link with grade performance. However, no significant association was identified between the motivational strategies and students' behavioral, emotional, or cognitive engagement. The study indicates that motivational strategies have some impact on students’ academic performance, but the effect is very limited. The study led to the development of the Science Motivation and Engagement Enhancement Program (SMEEP) as an intervention to improve students’ motivation, engagement, and academic achievement in Science. The program involves intrinsic and extrinsic motivational strategies through well-organized pre-assessment, implementation, and post-assessment activities.

items.title: Multimodal Evaluation of Exoskeleton Assistance Using Optimized Machine Learning
items.abstract: Repetitive manual material handling (MMH) remains a leading occupational risk factor for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSD), and passive shoulder-support exoskeletons have emerged as promising assistive technologies. Most evaluations rely on group-level statistics from single sensor modalities, leaving open whether their effects can be detected at the individual level. Thirty-five adults performed low-risk (4.54 kg, Lift Index (LI) < 1.0) lifting tasks, derived from the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation, with and without the passive shoulder exoskeleton support. Surface electromyography (sEMG), inertial measurement unit (IMU) kinematics, and NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) ratings were derived into a 34 feature vector and classified using four models under Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross Validation to ensure our models were not trained on already seen data. SVM with radial basis kernel reached 89.4% accuracy (AUC = 0.932) on low-risk lifting, Logistic Regression reached 84.8% (AUC = 0.904) on high-risk lifting. NASATLX physical demand proved to be the most important feature in permutation importance, outranking all biomechanical features. Perceived workload may be a more consistent cross-subject signal than objective biomechanics, with practical implications for low-burden field evaluation.

items.title: Occupational Health, Safety and Environmental Compliance and its Effects: A Case Study of Federal Polytechnic Bauchi, Nigeria
items.abstract: Occupational Health, Safety and Environmental (OHSE) compliance is a dynamic requirement for ensuring wellbeing, safety at work environments, curtailing work-related hazards and reassuring sustainable institutional procedures. This research evaluates the quality of OHSE compliance and its effects at Federal Polytechnic Bauchi, Nigeria. The study method adopted a cast study involving structured questionnaires, workplace adherences and inspection of safety-related documents. The study emphasized on safety observances, hazard regulatory procedures, personal protective equipment accessibility, emergency enthusiasm and environmental management routines. The findings demonstrate that effective OHSE compliance contributes significantly to accident prevention, better productivity, environmental safety and enhanced institutional sustainability. However, problems such as inadequate safety mindfulness, incoherent monitoring, inadequate safety resources and weak enforcement methods negate full compliance. The research recommends continuous safety training, enhanced inspection protocols, adequate provision of safety facilities (PPE), better-quality waste control systems and stronger institutional OHSE policies to intensify workshop safety and routine.

items.title: Responsive Digital Pedagogy for Elementary Learner Engagement
items.abstract: This study explored the predictive role of responsive digital pedagogy in shaping elementary learner engagement in Baggao, Cagayan. It focused on four dimensions of digital teaching: adaptive digital task design, responsive feedback, participatory digital interaction, and access-sensitive instructional support. An explanatory-predictive path design was applied to data from 90 public elementary school teachers selected through stratified criterion-random sampling. Responses were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, bootstrapping with 10,000 resamples, PLSpredict, and importance-performance map analysis. The measurement model established acceptable reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Results showed that responsive digital pedagogy explained 62.4% of the variance in learner engagement. Responsive feedback exerted the strongest positive effect, followed by participatory digital interaction and adaptive digital task design. Access-sensitive instructional support, however, did not significantly predict engagement and emerged as the weakest area of implementation. Predictive analysis further showed that the model performed better in explaining active participation, sustained attention, and learning effort than cognitive involvement. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of digital instruction depends less on technology use itself and more on how teachers adapt digital experiences, provide timely feedback, and create meaningful opportunities for participation. Strengthening access-sensitive practices and designing tasks that promote deeper cognitive engagement are recommended to improve responsive digital teaching in elementary classrooms.

items.title: Sampling Safe Futures: Multimodal Trajectory Planning for Personalized Safety in Anthropomorphic AI
items.abstract: Anthropomorphic artificial intelligence systems increasingly remember personal details, display empathy, and are engaged with as social counterparts, creating forms of risk that emerge from the evolution of the user-system relationship over time. Existing safeguards largely operate at the level of individual conversational turns and cannot determine whether a sequence of seemingly acceptable interactions is cumulatively moving a particular user toward harm. This paper introduces personalized trajectory-level safety, a framework that treats relational safety as a sequential decision problem over a latent escalation state inferred from the user's messages and influenced by the system's responses. At each turn, a screening step first discards any response strategy that does not preserve at least one safe continuation of the interaction under every plausible model of the user. Among the remaining strategies, we formulate action selection as multimodal trajectory sampling, and use a Generative Flow Network to generate diverse future evolutions in proportion to their plausibility, safety, and utility. The system then selects the strategy that preserves the largest fraction of safe and useful continuations. We evaluate the framework in simulation, calibrated on statistics reported for real human-chatbot interactions, and using response strategies derived from public benchmarks. Results show that trajectory-aware decision making substantially reduces the frequency of harmful states while keeping helpful interaction. This work reframes safety for anthropomorphic AI from response-level filtering to personalized control over the future evolution of human-AI relationships. The source code is available at https://github.com/benedettapicano/ANTHROPOMORPHIC_SAFETY_TRAJ.

items.title: Situational Awareness as a Human Factor in Near Miss and Crash Incidents Among Student Motorcyclists
items.abstract: Motorcycle riders are among the most vulnerable road users due to their direct exposure to dynamic traffic environments, while many traffic accidents are preceded by near-miss incidents that provide valuable opportunities for proactive safety evaluation. This study aimed to examine the effect of Situational Awareness (SA) on near-miss and crash incidents among university student motorcycle riders and to evaluate the contribution of the Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART) dimensions, namely Demand, Supply, and Understanding. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed involving 96 Universitas Malikussaleh students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on the SART instrument and analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression after confirming the validity and reliability of the instrument and the fulfillment of regression assumptions. The results demonstrated that Situational Awareness had a significant negative effect on both near-miss (β = −0.614, p < 0.001) and crash incidents (β = −0.370, p < 0.001), explaining 48.7% and 42.3% of the variance, respectively. Furthermore, the Understanding dimension consistently showed the strongest influence on both safety outcomes, whereas the Supply dimension was not significantly associated with crash incidents. These findings indicate that improving riders' cognitive ability to recognize, interpret, and anticipate hazardous traffic situations may contribute to reducing near-miss events and crash risks, providing practical implications for motorcycle safety education and hazard perception training among university students.

items.title: The IDEA Design Scaffold: A Developmental Framework for Functional Ideation in Systemic Design
items.abstract: Abstract Functional ideation in systemic design unfolds within sociotechnical and sociocultural environments where goals, constraints, and evaluative criteria evolve across multiple levels of organization. Creativity research explains important aspects of novelty, variation, recombination, and selective retention, but it often treats novelty as emerging within a relatively stable representational space or a single level of abstraction. Systemic design scholarship, in turn, has developed strong approaches for framing complexity, mapping relations, organizing participation, and coordinating action, but it less often specifies how designers navigate between systemic levels, address challenges at different levels of abstraction, and construct intervention candidates while the task environment is still being differentiated. This paper responds by proposing a naturalistic framework of ideation within the Interactivist–Constructivist paradigm, with the IDEA Design Scaffold as its methodological architecture for systemic design. The central claim is that functional ideation under systemic complexity must be understood as a self-directed developmental process: intervention opportunities become novel and appropriate as designers navigate across levels of complexity through anticipatory exploration, partial stabilization, reflective reorganization, and rebuilding of missing supports. IDEAS operationalizes this account by linking Systemic Breakdown and Systemic Integration through the Iterative Innovation Cycle, enabling systemic goals, design challenges, and intervention candidates to be progressively coordinated without reducing ideation to a fixed procedure. The payoff is both theoretical and methodological: the paper explains why creative development in systemic design requires movement across levels of complexity, and provides an architecture for supporting, studying, and refining that movement in systemic design practice.

items.title: The viral deviation: a quantitative analysis of social media engagement metrics on non-compliant flight deck behaviors
items.abstract: Background Normalization of Deviance (NoD) is a well-documented organizational failure mode in aviation, yet its propagation through digital ecosystems remains unexplored. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) highlights a critical mentorship vacuum due to pilot retirements, and social media platforms increasingly serve as informal training environments. This study introduces the concept of Algorithmic Normalization of Deviance- ANoD, hypothesizing that recommendation algorithms systematically reward and amplify “gray-zone” cockpit behaviors that erode sterile flight deck protocols. Method We conducted a stratified netnographic analysis of 150 high-visibility aviation videos (N = 150) across Instagram Reels, split between algorithmically recommended content (n = 100) and curated influencer content (n = 50). A novel coding framework operationalized compliance (Compliant vs. Gray Zone vs. Deviant) and incentive structures. Engagement metrics were analyzed to quantify the algorithmic advantage of non-compliant behavior. Results The analysis reveals a directionally consistent “Viral Deviation” pattern rather than a statistically decisive one. Gray-zone recordings (i.e., technically legal but procedurally borderline) comprised 57% of the sample and attracted higher engagement than compliant content, although this difference was small and did not reach conventional significance (d = 0.24, p = 0.11). The clearest signal emerged between content sources: algorithmically surfaced posts showed significantly higher interaction rates than curated influencer posts (d = 0.31, p = 0.029), a small but statistically significant per-view advantage for content promoted directly by the recommendation system. Structural incentive analysis further indicates that monetization pressures co-occur with increased gray-zone production, structurally analogous to a parallel, shadow curriculum associated with conditions that may facilitate drift. Conclusion The study identifies statistical associations, not causal relationships, and the downstream behavioural impact on pilots is hypothesised from the algorithmic-pattern evidence rather than directly measured. Within those bounds, social media algorithms constitute a structurally unmonitored distribution channel whose observed associations with gray-zone content amplification are consistent with a normalisation-of-deviance feedback mechanism operating beyond current regulatory oversight — an association that warrants urgent empirical validation and proactive governance. We propose a shift from prohibition to risk-stratified governance, recommending that regulators distinguish between handheld (high-risk) and mounted (managed-risk) devices, and integrate digital algorithmic literacy into ab-initio pilot training to counter this new systemic threat.

items.title: Virtual Reality Hypnosis: The Effectiveness of Virtual Reality Combined with Hypnotic Suggestions, a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used to support physical and mental health interventions. Recently, VR combined with hypnotic suggestions, termed virtual reality hypnosis (VRH), has emerged as a promising approach across clinical and non-clinical settings. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the use and effectiveness of VRH. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Embase following PRISMA guidelines. A total of 54 studies involving healthy and clinical populations were included. Meta-analytic results based on pre-post comparisons indicated a trend toward reduced anxiety following VRH (Hedges’ g = −1.39; 95% CI: −2.91 to 0.14). However, no significant differences were found when VRH was compared with other interventions, and no significant effects emerged for pain outcomes. Overall, VRH appears to be a promising intervention integrating immersive virtual environments with hypnotic suggestion, although further high-quality research is needed.

items.title: What occupational health challenges do hazmat truck drivers face? A network analysis and implications for safety management
items.abstract: Hazardous materials (hazmat) road transportation entails substantial safety risks, in which driver-related factors are consistently identified as the leading contributors to crashes. Yet the occupational profile, health status, and psychosocial resources of hazmat truck drivers remain poorly characterized, constraining the development of evidence-based safety management. To address this gap, this study surveyed 347 hazmat truck drivers in China, combining standardized scales with self-developed items capturing context-specific working experiences. These drivers were middle-aged (M = 42.52 years). The majority of them (87.6%) were overweight or obese. More than half of them were suffering musculoskeletal discomfort (58.8%) and suspected insomnia or insomnia (56.8%) together with daytime sleepiness. Although their self-reported fatigue was relatively low, sleep-related problems and physical health issues warrant particular attention. Network analysis further revealed two functionally distinct clusters within the work system: a physiological risk cluster (fatigue, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness) and a psychosocial resource cluster (perceived social support, professional identity, and subjective well-being). The associations between the two clusters were predominantly negative, suggesting a dynamic balance between occupational strain and adaptive resources. Subjective well-being, insomnia, and fatigue emerged as the most central nodes, indicating that they may serve as priority entry points for intervention. Our findings highlight that safeguarding the occupational health and safety of hazmat truck drivers requires an integrated and system-oriented management approach that jointly addresses physiological risks, psychosocial resources, and physical health. The study offers empirical evidence and practical implications for safety management in hazmat road transportation.

items.title: A Hybrid Risk Assessment Approach Using Fine-Kinney Method and Fault Tree Analysis for Enhancing Laboratory Safety
items.abstract: To enhance laboratory safety, a risk assessment was conducted in environmental engineering laboratories using the Fine-Kinney Method (FKM) and Fault Tree Analysis (FTA). The FKM was initially employed to prioritize hazards, with a subsequent FTA used to systematically identify root causes and evaluate the effectiveness of existing controls. These two complementary approaches identified 10 risks, categorized into four groups: physical (electricity, fire, falling, sharp object injury), chemical (acid, poisoning, contamination), biological (infection, allergy), and ergonomic (musculoskeletal injury). Post-control measures successfully eliminated 89.3% of ‘Not Tolerated’ risks, contributing to an overall 63% reduction across all high-priority categories, including ‘Not Tolerated,’ ‘Strong,’ and ‘Important’ risks in FKM. Application of the FTA led to substantial risk reductions, with post-control measures decreasing hazard scores for fire, acid exposure, and electricity by 72.8%, 66.5%, and 60.0%, respectively. The statistical validation of the findings confirmed that the risk reductions achieved in both the FKM and FTA models were highly significant. The alignment of risk rankings across both models validated the assessment's reliability, providing a robust foundation for decision-making. Finally, implementing these validated safety measures requires a total budget of $42,000.

items.title: A questionnaire survey on context-dependent requirements for the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence and humans
items.abstract: Trustworthiness has become an important focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research. Although trustworthiness is a multifaceted concept and its requirements may depend on the context in which AI is used, little is known about how the public perceives these requirements. To address this issue, we conducted a questionnaire survey with nonexpert participants to examine the requirements that the public considers important for trustworthy AI and how their perceived value differs between social and nonsocial contexts. We further compared these context-dependent patterns with those observed for human trustworthiness. Our findings showed that, across social and nonsocial contexts, confidentiality and privacy protection were among the most important requirements for AI trustworthiness whereas the relative importance of other requirements depended on the context. In nonsocial contexts, transparency and interpretability of decision-making were particularly important whereas in social contexts, the ability to collaborate and communicate and a positive public image and attractive appearance were predominantly significant. Although similar context-dependent patterns were observed for human trustworthiness, findings consistently highlighted the ability to collaborate and communicate as a requirement for trusting humans, regardless of context, in contrast to AI trustworthiness. These findings provide insights into the public’s perception of trustworthy AI and highlight the importance of considering the context in which AI is used when examining AI trustworthiness requirements.

items.title: AI and the layered evolution of information landscapes
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI has sparked debates about whether we are experiencing revolutionary disruption or evolutionary transformation of the information landscape. While headlines proclaim unprecedented changes, understanding AI's impact requires situating current developments within the evolution of how we have created, shared, and used information over centuries. We argue that generative AI represents not a radical break, but the latest interim layer in an evolving information landscape, progressing from pre‐digital systems through centralized computing, personal computing, the web, and social media. We outline the characteristics of each layer, including information infrastructures, information flows, and human roles. We discuss how layers have built upon predecessors while introducing novel challenges and opportunities: the web democratized publishing, social media enabled viral many‐to‐many networks, and generative AI now positions machines as co‐creators in hybrid intelligence systems. This means, rather than displacing earlier infrastructures, developments like generative AI add complexity to the information landscape, in which multiple layers coexist and interact. By recognizing both continuity and novelty in the evolution of our information infrastructure, we can more effectively navigate the generative AI era and ensure that technological advancement augments rather than replaces human agency, while preparing for the sociotechnical challenges it inevitably brings.

items.title: Analyzing Human Centered Industrial Engineering Approaches in Improving Productivity and Employee Wellbeing in Modern Production Systems
items.abstract: Modern production systems increasingly rely on automation, digitalization, and advanced technologies to improve productivity, yet these developments may generate physical, cognitive, and psychosocial challenges for employees. This study aims to analyze human-centered industrial engineering approaches in improving productivity and employee wellbeing within modern production systems. A qualitative library research approach was employed by examining relevant books, peer-reviewed journal articles, scientific publications, research reports, and previous studies. Data were collected through systematic literature review and analyzed using content analysis to identify patterns, relationships, and key findings related to human-centered engineering, productivity, and employee wellbeing. The findings indicate that human-centered approaches can support productivity through improved work-system design, ergonomics, human–technology interaction, employee participation, and reduced physical and cognitive workload. At the same time, these approaches contribute to employee wellbeing by addressing physical, cognitive, and psychosocial factors. The study concludes that integrating human-centered principles into industrial engineering provides a sustainable pathway for jointly optimizing productivity and employee wellbeing in modern production systems.

items.title: Association between students’ self-perceptions in physical education and out-of-school physical activity: the role of autonomous motivation
items.abstract: Both organized (OrPA) and unorganized physical activities (UnPA) offer known health benefits to adolescents. However, many youths are increasingly abandoning physical activity (PA). Research suggests that students’ self-perceptions in physical education (PE)—such as interest, perceived competence, and the value they assign to PE—may influence PA outside of school. Yet, it remains unclear whether these factors directly impact PA or do so through other variables, like autonomous motivation. This study explored whether autonomous motivation mediates the relationship between PE self-perceptions and engagement in OrPA and UnPA. A total of 1320 secondary students (average age 14.28) completed surveys measuring motivation and activity levels. Two mediation models were tested using the R Package GLM Mediation Model. Perceived competence was the only significant predictor of both OrPA and UnPA. Interest, importance, and tension had no direct effects. Both models showed full mediation through autonomous motivation, particularly via integrated and identified regulations. Intrinsic motivation was not a significant mediator. Findings suggest that students’ perceived competence in PE encourages out-of-school PA by enhancing motivation. PE teachers should promote self-awareness, educate on health benefits, and equip students to plan their own PA, thus fostering lasting motivation. Resumen Tanto las actividades físicas organizadas (OrPA) como las no organizadas (UnPA) ofrecen beneficios para la salud de los adolescentes. Sin embargo, muchos jóvenes abandonan cada vez más la actividad física (AF). Estudios sugieren que la percepción que los estudiantes tienen de la educación física (EF), como el interés, la competencia percibida y el valor que le asignan, puede influir en la AF fuera de la escuela. Sin embargo, aún no está claro si estos factores influyen directamente en la AF o lo hacen a través de otras variables, como la motivación autónoma. Este estudio quiere investigar si la motivación autónoma realiza un papel mediador entre las autopercepciones de la EF y la participación en OrPA y UnPA. Un total de 1320 estudiantes de secundaria (edad media de 14,28 años) completaron encuestas sobre niveles de motivación y AF. Se probaron dos modelos de mediación utilizando el paquete R GLM Mediation Model. La competencia percibida fue el único predictor significativo tanto de la OrPA como de la UnPA. El interés, la importancia y la tensión no tuvieron efectos directos. Ambos modelos mostraron una mediación completa a través de la motivación autónoma, en particular a través de regulaciones integradas e identificadas. La motivación intrínseca no fue un mediador significativo. Los resultados sugieren que la competencia percibida por los estudiantes en la educación física fomenta la AF fuera de la escuela al mejorar la motivación. Los profesores de educación física deberían promover la autoconciencia, educar sobre los beneficios para la salud y facilitar a los estudiantes herramientas para que planifiquen su propia AF, fomentando así una motivación duradera.

items.title: Beyond Simple Input-Output Assessment Tasks: Leveraging Automated Programming Assessment for Non-Trivial Courses
items.abstract: The public visibility of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is growing rapidly, driven by the positive impact of its applications across diverse fields of knowledge. In this new chapter, courses that cover the foundations of AI and machine learning become essential for understanding their role and potential in contemporary society. Therefore, understanding fundamental concepts and elementary algorithms through the close integration of theory with practice is essential in AI courses. In this essay, we report our experience designing machine learning exercises for automated assessment tools in programming. It is worth mentioning that we are not developing a novel form of automated grading system. Instead, we propose a perspective that frames machine learning problems as input-output assessment tasks. From this perspective, each exercise admits a unique and deterministic answer and enables automated programming assessment tools (e.g., VPL for Moodle, Codeforces, and MOJ) to effectively support AI education. We believe this essay can encourage instructors to foster educational innovation by adopting more dynamic and interactive approaches to AI courses that integrate theory and practice. Importantly, this essay does not introduce an innovation in the use of AI for education; rather, it introduces an innovative approach to improving the learning of AI, particularly, machine learning.

items.title: Beyond technical capability: how institutional resistance shapes generative AI exposure in civil and environmental engineering occupations
items.abstract: Purpose This article introduces the Integrated Sociotechnical Exposure Framework (ISEF) to assess generative AI exposure in civil and environmental engineering by separating technical AI suitability (TA) from institutional resistance (IR). The contribution is an operational measurement framework, not a claim that institutional constraint is a new concept. Design/methodology/approach The framework is applied to 674 O*NET tasks across 28 occupations. Task-variable pairs are scored by three large language models under a fixed rubric and then aggregated to occupation level. Exposure is modelled with a multiplicative form, and sensitivity checks compare additive, min-rule, and geometric alternatives. A small external practitioner survey is used as a calibration check rather than as task-level validation. Findings A large group of occupations score well on technical AI suitability but stay heavily constrained by liability, compliance, and sign-off requirements. The cleaned practitioner survey points in the same direction: across 15 task vignettes, higher perceived institutional constraint is strongly associated with lower adjusted AI exposure. Research limitations/implications The scoring still leans on LLMs, and the practitioner sample is small. Because no same-task expert panel is available in the present revision, the results should be read as a transparent first-stage index. The nine-response practitioner exercise is preliminary calibration, not validation of the occupation-level index or its constructed adjusted-score analogue. The natural next step is a larger same-task expert panel paired with adoption-linked field evidence. Practical implications For engineering organisations, adoption strategy is better anchored in accountable workflows, auditability, and professional review processes than in model capability on its own. Originality/value The paper pulls governance constraints into the exposure measure itself, and uses that lens to explain why technical-only indices tend to overstate near-term generative AI uptake in regulated engineering work. Its measurement logic is potentially transferable to other regulated professions, but any such application requires domain-specific specification and calibration of the institutional-resistance construct.

items.title: Boosting playful work design: a test of a micro and modular e-intervention
items.abstract: Purpose Playful work design (PWD) refers to approaching and performing work activities playfully to foster fun and challenge. In this study, we build on the idea that PWD stems from a malleable metacognitive competency that can be cultivated through intentional activities. Design/methodology/approach Accordingly, we developed and tested a micro (Study 1) and a modular PWD e-intervention (Study 2) aimed at nurturing the knowledge, skills and abilities central to PWD. Findings Results of Study 1 (N = 74 individuals, n = 432 days) revealed that actively completing exercises can promote designing competition but not designing fun. In Study 2, individuals who actively participated in the modular e-intervention increased in both designing fun and designing competition (N = 127 individuals; n = 549 weeks). In both studies, mere exposure to the e-intervention did not predict outcomes. Across both studies, PWD was positively related to creative performance through informal learning (Study 1) and self-efficacy (Study 2). Originality/value The findings highlight the promise of e-interventions in cultivating PWD, which can help to strengthen employees' creative performance.

items.title: Celebrity Endorsement in the AI Era: How Synthetic Endorsements Featuring Living and Deceased Celebrities Shape Brand Opportunism Across Campaign Purposes
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping how living and deceased celebrities can be represented and reused in media and marketplace communication. Yet little is known about how consumers respond to AI-generated celebrity representations. Drawing on attribution theory and social contract theory, this study employs a 2 (represented celebrity life status: living vs. deceased) × 2 (campaign type: commercial vs. prosocial) between-subjects experiment with 229 U.S. participants. Results showed no significant main effect of celebrity life status on perceived brand opportunism. Instead, a significant interaction effect emerged, and the use of a deceased celebrity increased opportunism perceptions only in commercial campaigns. Brand opportunism was negatively associated with purchase intention and attitudes toward the celebrity’s public image, but indirect effects emerged only in the commercial condition. The findings contribute to human-computer interaction, synthetic media, and AI-generated advertising research while offering practical guidance for more cautious and context-sensitive use of AI-generated celebrity endorsers.

items.title: Cognitive Load as a Hidden Cost of Empathy: Tradeoffs in Using VR for Inclusive Design
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is used to bridge the “empathy gap” in inclusive design, but whether emotionally evocative simulations improve design outcomes remains unclear. We conducted a between-subjects experiment comparing passive video with non-emotional and emotional interactive VR simulations of low-vision mobility challenges, informed by interviews and co-design with low-vision participants. Emotional intensity was manipulated via non-player-character feedback while task structure and task-relevant information were held constant. We measured empathy change and assessed design ideas by alignment with user-prioritized needs. Both VR conditions increased empathy relative to video, but emotional VR produced no additional measurable gain, whereas non-emotional VR produced stronger user-need-aligned ideation than both other conditions. Drawing on cognitive load theory, we propose that emotionally charged cues may introduce extraneous demands during ideation, offering a working hypothesis for this divergence. Our work provides guidelines for calibrating VR emotional intensity to balance empathic engagement and design ideation.

items.title: Communicating When Hazards Arrive: Adding Arrival Time Information to Hurricane Hazard Maps
items.abstract: Hurricane Threats and Impacts (HTI) graphics communicate the spatial extent and severity of tropical cyclone hazards but provide limited information about when hazards will arrive, creating challenges for time-sensitive protective decision-making. We evaluated whether adding arrival time information to redesigned HTI-like graphics improves temporal comprehension, influences risk perception and protective actions, and is perceived as usable. In a mixed-design experiment, 248 Florida residents from coastal and inland communities were randomly assigned to view graphics with or without arrival time bands (between-subjects) for three hurricane scenarios (within-subjects). Time bands significantly improved comprehension, increasing correct responses nearly six-fold from 7.0% to 40.8%. Without time bands, participants predominantly interpreted advisory issuance times as hazard arrival times. Temporal information did not affect risk perception or protective actions, which were driven primarily by tropical cyclone characteristics. Both designs received comparable usability ratings. Findings show temporal visualizations can begin to address comprehension deficits without compromising usability.

items.title: Comparing GenAI Summaries Versus Chatbots for Supporting Reflection in Healthcare Simulation
items.abstract: Reflection is critical for learning. In healthcare, simulations help learners practice clinical and teamwork skills, while reflection supports improving practice. Learning analytics (LA) dashboards can support reflection by visualizing activity data, but their effectiveness is limited by learners’ ability to interpret data visualizations and domain knowledge. Generative AI (GenAI) may bridge this gap through narrative explanations of data. Yet little is known about how forms of GenAI support—such as chatbots or summaries—affect reflection. We conducted a comparative study with 41 nursing students who wrote reflections after a simulation, supported by an LA dashboard augmented with a GenAI summary or chatbot. Results suggest that written reflections differed across conditions: GenAI summaries help align reflections with learning goals, while chatbots encourage consideration of actions and plans. However, nursing teachers identified no difference in the quality of plans. These findings suggest GenAI configuration may shape how technologies support reflection.

items.title: Computer Vision–Based monocular 3D human pose estimation and ergonomic risk assessment: The impact of model variants and camera views on kinematic accuracy and ergonomic assessment validity
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) remain highly prevalent and are a leading cause of occupational disability, underscoring the need for scalable and reliable ergonomic risk assessment methods. Although computer vision has shown great promise in automating human pose estimation and ergonomic risk evaluation, systematic evidence is still required to clarify how model variant, camera view, and occlusion affect both kinematic accuracy and ergonomic assessment outcomes. This study systematically compared two widely used open-source monocular 3D human pose estimation models, MediaPipe and MMPose , against an optical motion capture reference system across a series of static and dynamic tasks recorded from three camera views (front, 45°, and side). Results showed that MediaPipe achieved higher overall kinematic accuracy in estimating joint positions and angles, as well as stronger agreement with ergonomic risk assessment scores (REBA and RULA) than MMPose . MediaPipe achieved optimal performance at the 45° camera view for both joint estimation and ergonomic assessment, whereas MMPose performed best from the side view for pose estimation and the front view for ergonomic assessment. These findings clarify how pose-estimation accuracy translates into ergonomic assessment validity and provide practical guidance for applying computer vision–based methods to achieve accessible, scalable, and reliable ergonomic risk assessment in workplace settings.

items.title: DocuTeam: Mixed-Initiative Multi-Agent Discussions around Evolving Documents
items.abstract: In open-ended problem solving, collaborators often rely on discussion to surface concerns, challenge perspectives, and refine shared work as it evolves. While AI agents are increasingly used as discussion partners, existing multi-agent systems place a heavy burden on users to initiate and carefully orchestrate the discussions. We present DocuTeam, a mixed-initiative multi-agent discussion system in which both users and agents can initiate and steer conversations. Agents monitor document changes to proactively start and redirect discussions as the work evolves, while users can flexibly shape the conversation or adopt agent ideas. In a within-subjects study (N=20), participants using DocuTeam produced outcomes rated significantly more novel, relevant, and specific than with a baseline without any increase in cognitive load. Rather than using agents for one-off idea sourcing, participants engaged in an iterative refinement loop in which document changes prompted agent reactions, which led users to revisit and further develop their work.

items.title: Doping-related attitudes and intentions among Croatian athletes: Examining theory of planned behavior constructs and broader psychosocial correlates
items.abstract: Bacckground: Doping continues to pose persistent challenges in competitive sport. Although prior studies have investigated Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) constructs together with a range of psychosocial correlates of doping, evidence from large and heterogeneous athlete samples remains limited.Objective: This study provides a large-sample contextual replication and extension of previous TPB-based doping research by examining associations among TPB constructs, performance-enhancement attitudes, self-esteem, achievement goal orientation, sport motivation, descriptive norms, and self-reported use of prohibited substances for performance enhancement in 988 Croatian athletes from team and individual sports.Methods: Analyses included psychometric evaluation, descriptive statistics, bivariate correlations, group comparisons, and hierarchical multiple regression.Results: Overall, 7.6% of participants reported prohibited substance use at least once during their sporting careers. Male athletes reported more favorable doping-related and performance-enhancement attitudes and stronger behavioral intentions. Individual-sport athletes and athletes in the lower competition-level group more frequently reported lifetime prohibited-substance use. Higher self-esteem, stronger task orientation, and greater intrinsic motivation were associated with less favorable doping-related and performance-enhancement attitudes and weaker behavioral intentions, whereas lower self-esteem, ego orientation, extrinsic motivation, and amotivation were associated with more permissive attitudes and stronger behavioral intentions. Attitudes toward doping showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention, followed by performance-enhancement attitudes and subjective norms. The findings replicate previously established associations between TPB constructs and doping intention while extending the evidence base by demonstrating systematic associations with a broader set of psychosocial characteristics in a large sample of Croatian athletes.Conclusion: These findings provide context-specific evidence that may inform future longitudinal research and the development of psychosocially informed anti-doping interventions.

items.title: Effects of SA-Based Augmented Reality HUDs on Driver Situation Awareness in Level 3 ADS Under Adversarial Attack
items.abstract: An adversarial attack on Level 3 automated driving systems (ADS) introduces maliciously crafted perturbations to perception inputs, potentially leading to unsafe system decisions. To mitigate the safety risks posed by adversarial attacks and improve drivers’ situation awareness (SA) during takeover requests (ToR), this study proposes the implementation of SA-based augmented reality head-up displays (AR-HUDs). Forty participants took part in a laboratory experiment, completing a total of eight driving trials in a simulator under different SA-based AR-HUD conditions during adversarial attacks. Driver SA was measured using the Situation Awareness Global Assessment Technique, and data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The present study revealed a significant effect of AR-HUD condition on drivers’ overall SA during L3 ADS takeovers under a road-surface induced adversarial attack. The results offer design implications for future multimodal ToR systems, highlighting the importance of incorporating SA level-specific cues to support more effective SA recovery.

items.title: Emergence of Goal‐Directed Behaviors via Active Inference With Self‐Prior
items.abstract: Infants often exhibit goal-directed behaviors, such as reaching for a sensory stimulus, even when no external reward criterion is provided. These intrinsically motivated behaviors facilitate spontaneous exploration and learning of the body and environment during early developmental stages. Although computational modeling can offer insight into the mechanisms underlying such behaviors, many existing studies on intrinsic motivation focus primarily on how exploration contributes to acquiring external rewards. In this paper, we propose a novel density model for an agent's own multimodal sensory experiences, called the "self-prior," and investigate whether it can autonomously induce goal-directed behavior. Integrated within an active inference framework based on the free energy principle, the self-prior generates behavioral references purely from an intrinsic process that minimizes mismatches between average past sensory experiences and current observations. This mechanism is also analogous to the acquisition and utilization of a body schema through continuous interaction with the environment. We examine this approach in a simulated environment and confirm that the agent spontaneously reaches toward a tactile stimulus. Our study implements intrinsically motivated behavior shaped by the agent's own sensory experiences, demonstrating the spontaneous emergence of intentional behavior during early development. SUMMARY: Suggests a computational model for early intentional behavior, integrating body-schema formation and goal-directed actions under the free energy principle. Introduces a self-prior as an internal density model that drives the emergence of goal-directed behaviors without external rewards. Demonstrates spontaneous reaching for a sticker by minimizing mismatches between observed multimodal sensory inputs and the empirically acquired self-prior.

items.title: Ergonomic Design, Ease of Use and Aesthetics as Determinants of Employee Productivity in Hotel Operation
items.abstract: The study examined ergonomic Design, Ease of Use and Aesthetics as determinants of employee productivity in hotel operation. The study identified the influence of ease of use as ergonomic physical factor on employee productivity and examined the influence of aesthetics as ergonomic physical factor on employee productivity. The study adopted a descriptive survey approach and it covered a population of five hundred and seventy-three (573) employees of 37 registered hotels scattered across the 5 local government areas of Ebonyi South Senatorial Zone of Ebonyi State. Taro Yamane’s formula was used to select a sample size of two hundred and thirty-six (236) respondents from the population. Data used in the study were gathered using four-point rating scale questionnaire and literary works of past scholars were extensively reviewed by the researcher in order to have an in-depth of the topic under discussion. Collected data were presented and analyzed using descriptive statistic such as frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation. The decision rule for mean stated that any mean above 2.5 and above was considered positive. Regression analysis was used to run SPSS version 25 for hypotheses formulated for the study. The critical value from the SPSS output for hypotheses one is 0.956, while it is 0.967 for hypotheses two. Findings from the study showed that ease of use as ergonomic physical factor has a high significant relationship with employee productivity in hotel operation. The study also revealed that a significant relationship exists between aesthetics as ergonomic physical factor and employee productivity in hotel operation. The study showed that proper use of equipment and work environment in hotel operation increase efficiency and effectiveness, make work faster, decrease in errors and mistakes, increase employee motivation and job satisfaction and reduce wastage. The study also revealed that a well aesthetics workspace enhances creativity and innovation among employees, adequate lighting improves productivity, adequate ventilation increases productivity, aesthetically workspace reduce distraction and improve workflow efficiency. The study concluded that ease of use and aesthetics as ergonomic physical factors improves overall employee’s productivity in hotel operations. The study recommended that equipment, tools, machines and workstations should be made to be in good shape in order to increase efficiency and effectiveness in terms of productivity, make production fast and accurate, decrease errors and mistakes during production in hotel operations. Workplace environment should be designed in such a way as to enhance creativity and innovation among employees, improve high level of productivity and reduce distraction and also make workflow more effective.

items.title: Evaluating In-Vehicle Drunk-Driving Warning Symbols Using Generative AI: A Comparison with Human Judgments
items.abstract: This study examined whether Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can evaluate in-vehicle drunk-driving warning symbols (telltales) in ways comparable to human perceptual and semantic judgments. Using visibility and intuitiveness ratings collected from Korean and Texas-based U.S. participants, the same 30 telltales were evaluated by GPT-4o and GPT-5.5. Pearson correlation and agreement analyses revealed significant positive associations between AI and human evaluations for both metrics, with stronger correspondence in intuitiveness. Symbols with clear meanings, simple structures, and familiar alcohol-, vehicle-, or prohibition-related cues received consistently favorable ratings from both AI and humans. These results suggest that AI judgments may be associated with symbolic meaning as well as visual form, supporting its potential as a preliminary evaluation tool. In early design stages of safety-critical domains such as drunk-driving prevention, AI may help prescreen visual designs, improve evaluation efficiency, strengthen preliminary design review, and support human-centered telltale development for practical vehicle interfaces.

items.title: Factors Influencing the Acceptance and Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies among University Lecturers in Thailand
items.abstract: Aim/Purpose: The primary objective of this study was to examine the factors that influence the acceptance and practical application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies among university lecturers in Thailand. By adopting the Extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) as the analytical framework, the study sought to identify how individual perceptions, motivational factors, social influences, and institutional conditions jointly shape lecturers’ behavioral intention to use AI and their actual usage behavior. The findings are expected to provide empirical insights that support strategic planning for sustainable AI integration in higher education. Introduction/Background: Artificial Intelligence has increasingly emerged as a transformative force in higher education, reshaping instructional practices, research processes, and academic administration. AI-driven applications such as adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, and learning analytics have expanded the potential for personalized and data-informed education. In Thailand, national development agendas, particularly Thailand 4.0 and the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2022–2027), have emphasized the importance of AI adoption to enhance workforce competencies and educational quality. Within this policy context, university lecturers play a critical role as key agents who translate technological initiatives into classroom practice and institutional outcomes. However, the successful integration of AI in higher education depends not solely on technological availability but primarily on lecturers’ acceptance, readiness, and the support structures provided by institutions. Understanding the psychological and organizational factors that influence lecturers’ decisions to adopt AI is therefore essential for effective policy implementation and institutional management. Methodology: In this study, a quantitative research approach was employed using a cross-sectional survey design. The target population consisted of full-time lecturers employed at public and private universities across Thailand. A total of 400 respondents were selected through stratified random sampling to ensure representation across institution types and academic disciplines. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire developed from established UTAUT2 measurement scales and adapted to the context of AI usage in higher education. The instrument underwent expert validation and reliability testing prior to data collection. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize respondent characteristics and variable levels. In contrast, multiple regression analysis was used to examine the relationships between the independent variables—Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Social Influence, Facilitating Conditions, Hedonic Motivation, Pprice Value, and Habit—and the dependent variables—Behavioral Intention and Use Behavior. Findings: The results indicated that university lecturers in Thailand generally reported high levels of intention to use AI technologies and moderate to high levels of actual usage. Regression analysis revealed that Performance Expectancy, Hedonic Motivation, Social Influence, and Habit had a statistically significant positive influence on Behavioral Intention to adopt AI. Together, these factors explained 61.2% of the variance in behavioral intention. In contrast, Effort Expectancy and Price Value did not demonstrate a significant effect on intention in this context. Regarding actual use behavior, Behavioral Intention emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by Facilitating Conditions and Habit. These variables collectively explained 48.7% of the variance in AI use behavior. The findings suggest that lecturers are more likely to adopt AI when they perceive clear professional benefits, derive enjoyment from using AI tools, experience supportive social norms, and have prior experience with digital technologies. At the same time, institutional support plays a crucial role in enabling sustained application. Contribution/Impact on Society: This study contributes to the academic literature by empirically validating the UTAUT2 model within the context of Thai higher education and AI adoption. It highlights the importance of both utilitarian and intrinsic motivational factors, demonstrating that lecturers value enjoyment and perceived usefulness more strongly than ease of use. The findings have practical implications for policymakers and university administrators by emphasizing that AI adoption strategies should move beyond basic technology provision to foster engaging, supportive, and habit-forming environments that encourage long-term use. Recommendations: Higher education institutions should prioritize communication strategies that clearly demonstrate the practical benefits of AI for teaching, research, and administrative tasks in order to enhance performance expectancy. In addition, universities should design engaging professional development activities—such as hands-on workshops, innovation labs, and collaborative experimentation—to stimulate hedonic motivation. Adequate technical infrastructure, training opportunities, and ongoing support services should also be ensured to strengthen facilitating conditions and enable lecturers to translate intention into actual use. Research Limitations: This study was subject to several limitations. The cross-sectional design restricted the ability to capture changes in lecturers’ attitudes and behaviors over time. Furthermore, reliance on an online survey may have limited participation by lecturers with lower levels of digital proficiency, potentially affecting the generalizability of the findings. Future Research: Future studies should adopt longitudinal research designs to examine the evolution of AI adoption behavior over time. Incorporating qualitative methods, such as interviews or focus groups, would also provide deeper insights into lecturers’ concerns, expectations, and contextual challenges related to AI usage. Comparative studies across academic disciplines or institutional types are recommended to refine the understanding of AI adoption dynamics in higher education.

items.title: Filling in the Gaps: A Rapid Scoping Review of Baseline Performance Measures for Prototype Design
items.abstract: This Rapid Scoping Review investigates the extent to which researchers have used commercial, mainstream video game counterparts of serious games for calibration, establishing a baseline performance measure for Extraneous Cognitive Load. The findings from the Rapid Scoping Review will be used to address any identified methodological gaps and to propose mapping and implementing a pedagogically grounded framework or guidelines for serious game prototype design to improve Working Memory efficiency for researchers investigating the effectiveness of serious games. Moreover, the inferences from the framework or guidelines may expand upon or contribute to knowledge and methodological approaches related to the transfer of learning, more specifically, near transfer. Establishing accurate baseline metrics to assess the effectiveness of serious games is essential for sound instructional design and meaningful research outcomes. Therefore, mapping the current knowledge gap and identifying existing methodologies for baseline performance indicators is essential. This study will follow PRISMA-ScR guidelines to conduct a comprehensive literature search across three primary databases: Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ERIC. The screening process will target empirical studies that explicitly discuss cognitive load and employ empirical baseline or calibration measurements (e.g., physiological sensors, subjective scales, or dual-task paradigms) in research on serious games or commercial, mainstream video games. Data extraction will be conducted by a single reviewer and a second reviewer for a random 10% of records, using 100% human-verified Large Language Model assistance for preliminary parsing, to synthesize thematic approaches to calibration, cognitive load measurement methods, and database-specific contributions.
